props.title: Borsalino and Co.

sections.content: **Borsalino and Co. (1974)** (1974) serves as Jacques Deray's gritty follow-up to the original Borsalino (1970), with Alain Delon returning to the criminal underworld of 1930s Marseille. While the first film paired Delon with Jean-Paul Belmondo in a charismatic buddy dynamic, this darker sequel follows Delon's character Roch Siffredi on a brutal revenge mission after his partner's murder. The film exemplifies the distinctive French crime film tradition that influenced later works like **The Professional** (1994) and **A Prophet** (2009), blending stylish period atmosphere with unflinching violence.

sections.content: The 1970s marked a pivotal evolution in French crime cinema, moving away from the romantic gangster mythology of the 1960s toward grittier realism. **Borsalino and Co.** reflects this shift through its vengeful protagonist and unflinching violence. The film shares DNA with Jean-Pierre Melville's stark crime masterpieces like **Le Cercle Rouge** (1970) and Un Flic (1972), while maintaining the period glamour and criminal empire scope of classics like **Once Upon a Time in America** (1984).

Director Jacques Deray and Alain Delon collaborated on several influential crime films including The Swimming Pool (1969) and **Three Men to Kill** (1980). Their partnership helped define the sophisticated yet ruthless French gangster archetype that influenced international crime cinema. **Borsalino and Co.** represents their most ambitious period piece, recreating 1930s Marseille with meticulous detail while delivering hard-edged action sequences that would influence later European crime thrillers. sections.content: The 1970s shift in French crime films mirrors broader changes in European cinema, moving from the stylized approach of the French New Wave toward a grittier aesthetic. Films like **The French Connection** (1971) and **Mean Streets** (1973) influenced this new wave of realistic crime dramas. **Borsalino and Co.** bridges both worlds - maintaining period glamour while embracing graphic violence and moral ambiguity that would become hallmarks of modern crime cinema.
